slides.heading: Bubble Sort
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Easy · Sorting
slides.narration: Let's solve Bubble Sort, an easy sorting problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order pairs; stop early when a pass makes no swaps.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order pairs; stop early when a pass makes no swaps.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Repeatedly swap neighbours that are out of order; each pass bubbles the largest remaining item to the end.
slides.narration: Repeatedly swap neighbours that are out of order; each pass bubbles the largest remaining item to the end.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Bubble sort is O(n²) — fine for learning, not for production
Better: merge/quick/heap sort → O(n log n)
Early exit makes sorted input O(n)
slides.narration: Bubble sort is quadratic, so in practice you'd use an n log n sort. Its one strength is the early exit: if a pass makes no swaps, the array is sorted, so already-sorted input takes linear time.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Loop until a pass makes no swaps
2. Swap adjacent pairs that are out of order
slides.narration: Step by step. First, loop until a pass makes no swaps. Second, swap adjacent pairs that are out of order. Third, shrink the range each pass.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: The outer loop repeats until no swaps happen. The inner loop compares each adjacent pair and swaps if out of order, and the range shrinks by one each pass.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n squared worst, O of n best. Space is constant.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Shrink the inner range each pass
Stop when a pass makes no swaps
slides.narration: Shrink the range each pass and stop early when nothing swaps. Bubble sort is stable, so equal elements keep their order.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Know the complexity of all simple sorts
Follow-up: why is it stable? how many swaps = inversions?
slides.narration: Be ready to compare it with insertion and selection sort. The number of swaps equals the number of inversions.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Repeatedly swap neighbours that are out of order; each pass bubbles the largest remaining item to the end.
slides.narration: To recap Bubble Sort: Repeatedly swap neighbours that are out of order; each pass bubbles the largest remaining item to the end. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
